text:
sara: Heads up — canary shows a CPU regression on the tokenization + prefetch path. Flamegraph spikes in Python/GIL frames around tokenizer and prefetch worker.
jamie: Yikes. Which perf commands did you run?
sara: Repro steps:
```
sudo perf record -F 99 -p $(pgrep -f redwood-runtime) -g -- sleep 30
perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
./flamegraph.pl out.folded > /tmp/flame-sara.svg
```
sara: Flame shows stacks mapping to PyEval_EvalFrameEx -> tokenizer._tokenize_batch -> Prefetcher._process_item -> scheduler.tick.
perf-bot: Uploaded flamegraph: https://perf-artifacts.company/sara/1953456789/flame-sara.svg :eyes:
mike: Do you have perf.data or the folded file? stackcollapse can hide some frames.
sara: uploaded out.folded and perf script snippets to perf-artifacts. Snippet: 
```
  sample 12345/ac: PyEval_EvalFrameEx; tokenizer.py:182; prefetch.py:58; scheduler.py:321
  sample 12346/ac: PyThreadState_Get; PyEval_EvalFrameEx; prefetch.py:62
```
cheng: Quick thought: the KV prefetch worker parses metadata in Python while holding a lock before putting into KV. That could be GIL contention. Also possible kernel-selection fallback is shifting work to CPU for short sequences.
jamie: Can we run py-spy to get pure-Python stacks (non-root friendly) so we see exact Python frames without frame-unwind noise?
sara: Ran py-spy for 20s — shows repeated tokenizer._tokenize_batch and Prefetcher._process_item holding a lock.
mike: If Prefetcher holds a lock during parse or I/O, it serializes tokenization. Can you paste the Prefetcher code?
cheng: Snippet from prefetcher.py: 
```
class Prefetcher:
    def _process_item(self, item):
        with self._lock:
            meta = self._parse_metadata(item)
            self._kv_cache.put(meta.key, meta.val)
```
cheng: That lock around parse+put is suspicious. Parsing allocates Python objects and should be moved outside the lock or executed in a thread/process pool.
jamie: Agreed — move parse out of the lock and only acquire for the put. For tight paths, implement parsing in a C extension or use a process pool to avoid GIL.
mike: Also check batching heuristics. If batcher emits many small batches (high batch frequency), prefetch overhead and GIL contention increases.
sara: I toggled REDWOOD_BATCH_MAX_TOKENS=4096 on canary — regression disappears. With default 512 the spike reproduces. So small batches amplify the issue.
cheng: That fits: small batches => more prefetch calls => more lock contention. Mitigations: increase default batch size, decouple parse into worker pool, or make Prefetcher put path lock-free (CAS-based).
jamie: For kernel selection, run an nsys timeline to see if we’re using fused GPU kernels or falling back to CPU for short sequences; nsys will show long CPU stalls between short GPU kernels.
sara: I captured an nsys trace earlier — timeline shows short kernels but 2-4ms CPU-side stalls coinciding with prefetch activity. Trace: https://perf-artifacts.company/sara/1953456789/nsys-timeline.qdrep
perf-bot: nsys trace uploaded.
mike: Next steps:
- cheng: move parse out of lock and add microbenchmark for prefetch path.
- jamie: run py-spy + perf side-by-side and produce a combined folded file (folded_with_py.txt) for a clearer flamegraph.
- sara: run canary with REDWOOD_BATCH_MAX_TOKENS=1024 and REDWOOD_PREFETCH_THREADS=0 to validate.
cheng: I'll open a small PR that moves parsing outside the lock and replace the critical section with: acquire lock; put into KV; release lock. Add a unit microbenchmark that simulates high batch frequency.
jamie: Add perf markers around the prefetch path (tracepoints or perf_event markers) to make grep in perf script easy.
mike: If CPU kernels persist after the lock change, enable DEBUG_KERNEL_SELECTION logs — maybe quantized kernel fallback for seq_len<8 triggers extra CPU pre/postprocessing.
sara: Running experiments now. I'll post short results and attach new flamegraphs/nsys traces. Thanks all :thumbsup:
